posts.name: dpt
posts.cooked:
The crew of La Paradoja Magnifica are:

[list]
[] The Amazing Mable, Mable Griffin. The use of “sugar” in the flavor text sounds pretty American to me. She is a flying trapeze artist, which according to Wikipedia was introduced around 1860 in France.
[] Final Breath, Ishikawa Zenjirou Kagemune. Pretty obviously Japanese. Ronins were active in the feudal Japan period, 1185-1868.
[] Chip, Charles “Chip” Stevenson. Flight goggles, scarf, and gun look WWI or WWII.
[] L’Épéiste, Pierre le Vignierz. Obviously French, but “Vignierz” is a pretty wierd name to me; does anyone know more? The Eiffel Tower, which seems to be under construction in his background, was constructed 1887-1889.
[] Battle Forged, Orinn Haugen, Scandinavian. The Viking age was ~790-1066.
[] Trueshot, Khutulan Bekhi. The names are Mongolian, but I don’t know enough to say more.
[*] Siege-Breaker, Geremio Esaltazione del Signore. Spanish name, right? The glasses look a little anachronistic

posts.name: dpt
posts.cooked:
Ameena:

If Chip was supposed to be a posh English guy I'd expect there to be no apostrophe - "cracking" instead of "crackin'".

The phenomenon usually called "g-dropping" (which is really a misleading name) occurs (as far as I know) in all varieties of modern English at all registers, although at varying frequencies. See  http://itre.cis.upenn.edu/~myl/languagelog/archives/000878.html .  That article mentions studies on American English, but I believe British dialects are similar in this regard.

Of course it's very weird for us to be speaking as though there were a single way British people speak, and, you know, not all people living in the UK are upper class with the nice tea cups.

posts.name: Silverleaf
posts.cooked:
The dropped G is really what breaks the stereotype for me. He's a WW2 fighter pilot by the look of him, and stereotypically they're upper class and therefore speak very correctly with all their Gs intact. (I know that in real life that's not the case - airmen came from all walks of life - but the trope is of the dashing posh chap from a public school (which for you non-Brits is actually a private school - don't ask). Think Lord Flashheart from Blackadder, or Ace Rimmer from Red Dwarf.)

I suppose my thought process is: if he's a fighter pilot and English he's posh. He drops the G so he isn't posh. Therefore he probably isn't English. Unless he's trying to "pass" for posh and not quite managing it?

If he'd said "hallo" instead of "hello" that would totally say English-from-that-time-period.

posts.name: dpt
posts.cooked:
Spiff:

Maybe Final Breath isn't obviously Japanese to a Japanese person.  Anyone here Japanese?

I'm not Japanese, and only speak enough Japanese to ask directions sometimes.  But the name is perfectly Japanese: Ishikawa Zenjirou Kagemune,  石川  善次郎  景宗.  All three components are names used by real people.  Ishikawa seems to be a clan name from the correct era:  Ishikawa clan - Wikipedia

 

I'm guessing Paul knows Japanese.  The calligraphy on Mr. Fixer's style cards looks not bad to my eyes, and appears to be done with a Japanese/Chinese calligraphy brush.  (Again, I don't speak Japanese, so can't give a verdict better than "not bad".)

 

Update: I read a little more, and learned that Japanese names were substantially different before the Meiji Restoration in the late 19th century, and I can't vouch for any sort of correctness.

phantaskippy:

That Pauline got it this time (for the only female Legacy, and only known female carrier of the genes) could have something to do with Elizabeth.

Speaking of which, while I wouldn't automatically go to this place with just any female hero, the fact that the Legacies are specifically a bloodline makes me think about Pauline being pregnant.  Would she continue to crimefight in that condition, and risk losing the baby if "Baroness Blade" or whoever gets in a really good whompf on her?  Or would she retire from superheroing for at least those nine months, leaving America without a Parsons hero for the first time since the 1770s?  Either way, I see drama.

Silverleaf:

If it wasn't for YL I'd suggest that maybe the trait is dominant and Y-linked and the firstborns all happened to be male and thus inherited the super Y chromosome from their father, and that they were either an only child or al subsequent children were either female, or illegitimate (i.e. with a different father which is not at all uncommon), or both. But of course Baby Legacy blows that theory out of the water, since she's female and doesn't have a Y chromosome but obviously has the superpower genes.

Actually it IS possible for a person who is apparently a woman to actually have a Y chromosome (or an apparent man to lack it, I think, though I only have confirmation of the former).  There are several disorders which can cause this; the one I'm most familiar with is called Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome, where the hormones that are supposed to cause male development in the fetus fail to work, and the child develops as physically female despite having XY genes.  Of course, this tends to lead to fertility problems, which could be a BIG issue in terms of America having another Legacy after her.
